extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, patent agents, judges, and law students (Canadian patent practice)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on legal tests and factors for assessing obviousness in Canadian patent law (including comparative discussion of U.K. and U.S. tests and the Sanofi refinement). Intended to inform litigation and patentability analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cripps question (obviousness for chemistry)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Was it obvious to any skilled chemist in the state of chemical knowledge existing at the date of the patent that he could manufacture valuable therapeutic agents by making the higher resorcinols by the use of the condensation and reduction processes described. If the answer is ‘No’ then the patent is valid, if ‘Yes’ the patent is invalid.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a practical formulation of the obviousness inquiry in chemical cases: asks whether a person skilled in the art, given the prior art and common general knowledge at the date, would have found the claimed solution plain. Quoted and applied in Canadian cases (e.g., Hoescht).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pope Appliance principle: first applicant entitlement / independent discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: “… what is invention? It is finding out something which has not been found out by other people. … There are many instances in various branches of science of independent investigators making the same discovery. That does not prevent the one who first applies and gets a patent from having a good patent …”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle that independent discovery by others does not defeat the first applicant's right to a patent; the focus remains on whether the subject-matter was previously found or was new to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unimaginative skilled technician / 'man in the Clapman omnibus' test
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether, in light of the state of the art and common general knowledge as at the claimed date of invention, the mythical skilled person would have 'come directly and without difficulty to the solution taught by the patent' (Hugessen J.A. wording).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the claimed invention would have been plain to an unimaginative technician given prior art and common general knowledge. Emphasis on 'directly and without difficulty' — not whether someone could eventually have achieved it after extensive exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: UK 'obvious to try' (Saint-Gobain): expectation of success / self-evident it ought to work
rubrics_metrics.description: Lord Justice Jacob: the 'obvious to try' test really only works where it is more or less self-evident that what is being tested ought to work; mere possible inclusion in a research programme is not enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the revised U.K. approach, an invention being 'obvious to try' is insufficient unless there is an expectation of success — it must be essentially self-evident that the trialled approach ought to work.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. 'obvious to try' (In re O'Farrell): reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: For obviousness under §103 all that is required is a reasonable expectation of success; absolute predictability is not necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court identifies two situations where 'obvious to try' might nonetheless be unobvious: (1) where one would vary many parameters without indication which are critical; (2) where prior art only gives general guidance for exploring a new technology. The U.S. test focuses on 'reasonable expectation of success' rather than certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR factor: design need/market pressure and finite predictable solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is a design need or market pressure to solve a problem and there are a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, a person of ordinary skill has good reason to pursue the known options; if this leads to the anticipated success it may indicate obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR rejects overly rigid TSM tests; in contexts with predictable solutions and market pressure, the fact that a combination was 'obvious to try' can support a finding of obviousness under §103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanofi general: Canadian 'obvious to try' requires predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanofi (Supreme Court of Canada) held that in cases where advances are often won by experimentation an 'obvious to try' test may be appropriate, but it requires predictability — one must have been able to predict that the alleged invention would work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canadian approach converges with U.K. and U.S. law: mere worth-a-try or possibility is insufficient; predictability that the approach would work is required when employing an 'obvious to try' inquiry (often applied as step four of Windsurfing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanofi factor 1: 'more or less self-evident' / finite predictable solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Is it 'very plain' or 'more or less self-evident' that what is being tried ought to work? Are there a finite number of identified predictable solutions known to persons skilled in the art?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This language is a synonym for 'readily apparent' or 'predictable' — ask whether, at the relevant date, one could predict that the claimed solution would work. If success was predictable, the claim leans toward obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanofi factor 2: extent, nature and amount of effort required
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the extent, nature and amount of effort required to achieve the invention? Are routine trials carried out or is the experimentation prolonged and arduous, such that the trials would not be considered routine?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art provides means and predicted results so that the inventor only needed routine verification, the invention is more likely obvious; prolonged, arduous, or non-routine experimentation weighs against obviousness (examples: Ratiopharm — routine salt screening found obvious; contrast Sanofi where arduous/uncertain work pointed against obviousness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanofi factor 3: motive provided in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a motive provided in the prior art to find the solution the patent addresses?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that prior art motivated skilled persons to pursue the claimed solution supports obviousness; absence of such motivation (or teaching away) supports non-obviousness. See chapter references on 'motivation: the climate of the invention.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of direct evidence from the invention team
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sanofi decision approved the use of direct evidence from the invention team itself in assessing obviousness (including whether success could be predicted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may consider testimony and documentary evidence from inventors about their research path and expectations (e.g., sound prediction evidence) when assessing whether the solution was predictable or whether the invention was obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: 'worth a try' (mere possibility) vs. predictability ('ought to work')
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere possibility that something might turn up is not enough; the proper inquiry is whether it would have been self-evident or predictable that the claimed invention would work, not merely that it was worth trying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'worth a try' test (English older approach) is inadequate for Canadian law post-Sanofi. Courts repeatedly caution that mere possibility or that someone 'might have' arrived at the invention does not render the invention obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirmatory and predictable experiments are not inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirmatory and predictable experiments that simply verify known or predicted results are not inventive and do not support patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When prior art already predicts results and the inventor merely verifies them by routine testing, courts may treat those experiments as non-inventive confirmation (see cross-references to earlier chapter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations: commercial success (long-felt need, adoption, sales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success is a secondary factor when considering obviousness: Was the invention quickly and anxiously received by relevant consumers? Had there been a long-felt need? Was the product widely adopted and did it have good sales?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where there is strong evidence of long-felt need and commercial success/acceptance, this may weigh against obviousness; useful cross-examination question: 'If it was so obvious, then why didn’t you think of it?' (court authorities cited for weighing commercial success).
